parts.problem_md: Define an oscillation.
parts.solution_md:
An oscillation is:

- Repeated back and forth movements; **[1 mark]**
- On either side of any equilibrium position;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problem_md:
Identify the correct definition by drawing lines between the properties of oscillations and their definition.

| **Properties of Oscillations** | **Definition of Properties** |
|---|---|
| Displacement | The rate of change of angular displacement with respect to time |
| Amplitude | The distance of an oscillator from its equilibrium position |
| Angular Frequency | The time taken for one complete oscillation |
| Frequency | The maximum displacement of an oscillator from its equilibrium position |
| Time Period | The number of oscillations per unit time |

parts.problem_md: Define simple harmonic oscillation.
parts.solution_md:
Simple harmonic oscillation is:

- A type of oscillation in which the acceleration of a body; **[1 mark]**
- Is proportional to its displacement; **[1 mark]**
- But acts in the opposite direction; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problem_md:
A pendulum undergoes small-angle oscillations.

State and explain the equation that defines simple harmonic motion.
parts.solution_md:
The defining equation for simple harmonic motion is:

- $a\propto-x$* ***[1 mark]**
- Where $a$ = acceleration **AND** $x$ = displacement (from equilibrium); **[1 mark]**

Explain what the equation means:

- Acceleration and displacement are directly proportional; **[1 mark]**
- Acceleration and displacement must always be in <u>opposite directions</u>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *Whenever you state an equation, it is important to define the **variables**. With simple harmonic motion, remember that not only does the negative sign mean that the vectors have opposite directions, but since displacement is measured away from the **equilibrium** position, acceleration must always be towards it.*

parts.problem_md:
The time taken for 10 oscillations is found to be 12.0 s.

Determine the frequency of the oscillation.
parts.solution_md:
Determine the frequency of the oscillation:

List the known quantities:

- Time taken for 10 oscillations = 12.0 s

Determine the period, *T:*

- $T=\frac{\mathrm{total} \mathrm{time} \mathrm{taken}}{\mathrm{number} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{oscillations}}=\frac{12.0}{10}$ = 1.2 s **[1 mark]**

Use the equation for frequency and period:

- Frequency:*  *$f=\frac{1}{T}$ **[1 mark]**
- Substitute:  $f=\frac{1}{1.2}$
- $f$ = 0.83 Hz **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Always set out your known quantities and immediately look for any conversions which may be required. Doing this at the start allows you space to notice, for example, that the question gave the time for 10 oscillations, not one, so you know you need to find the average value.*

A small wooden cuboid block of mass m floats in water. The top face of the block is horizontal and has an area A. The density of the water is ρ. The block is displaced downwards so that the surface of the water is now higher up the block.

The block in **(a) **is now released so that is oscillates vertically.

The resultant force *F *acting on the block is given by

$F=-Agρx$

where *g *is the gravitational field strength and *x *is the vertical displacement of the block from the equilibrium position.

Explain why the oscillations of the block are simple harmonic motion.
parts.solution_md:
The oscillations of the block are simple harmonic because:

- The area *A *,density *ρ, * and *g are constant,* so the force *F *is proportional to displacement *x* **[1 mark]**
- *F *and *x *act in opposite directions **[1 mark]****[Total: 2 marks]**

> *Link this equation to the **defining equation** of SHM. *

$a=-ω^{2}x$

> *This is negative because the object will **accelerate towards the centre** of the motion as **displacement is reduced**. *

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

The block in (a) is now released so that it oscillates vertically. The resultant force F acting on the block is given by F = -Agρx where g is the gravitational field strength and x is the vertical displacement of the block from the equilibrium position.

A small wooden cuboid block of mass m floats in water. The top face of the block is horizontal and has an area A. The density of the water is ρ.

Use the equation from **(b) **to obtain an expression for the angular frequency *ω* of the oscillations of the block.
parts.solution_md:
Obtain an expression for the angular frequency *ω* of the oscillations of the block:

Consider Newton's Second Law to obtain an expression for the acceleration of the block:

- $F=ma$
- So, $a=\frac{F}{m}=\frac{-Agρx}{m}$ **[1 mark]**

Consider the equation for centripetal acceleration:

- $a=rω^{2}$
- Where, *x *is the radius of the oscillation
- $a=-ω^{2}x$ **[1 mark]**

Combine the two equations for acceleration, *a*:

- $-ω^{2}x=\frac{-Agρx}{m}$
- $ω^{2}=\frac{Agρ}{m}$
- $ω=\sqrt{\frac{Agρ}{m}}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

A small metal pendulum bob is suspended at rest from a fixed point with a length of thread of negligible mass. Air resistance is negligible. The pendulum begins to oscillate. Fig. 1.1 shows the variation of kinetic energy of the pendulum bob with time.

![6-2-s-q--q5a-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](assets/010-6-2-s-q-q5a-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

[1]

where *l*  is the pendulum length and *g*  is the acceleration of free fall.

[2]
parts.solution_md:

A pendulum consists of a bob (small plastic sphere) attached to the end of a piece of wire. The other end of the wire is attached to a fixed point. The bob oscillates with small oscillations about its equilibrium position, as shown in Fig. 1.1.

parts.problem_md:
A mass of 0.42 kg is attached to a spring and the system is made to oscillate with simple harmonic motion (SHM) on a horizontal, frictionless surface. The mass passes through the equilibrium position 200 times per minute.

The kinetic energy of the mass as it passes through the equilibrium position is 500 mJ. There are two points where the restoring force acting on the mass is at its maximum.

Show that the distance between these points is approximately 29 cm.
parts.solution_md:
List the known quantities:

- Mass, *m* = 0.42 kg
- Passes through equilibrium 200 minute<sup>–1</sup>
- Kinetic Energy at *x* = 0, $E_{k}$= 500 mJ = 0.5 J

Determine the time period of the mass:

- The mass passes through the equilibrium position twice in one time period

  - There are 100 complete oscillations per minute
- *T* = $\frac{1}{f}$where *f* = $\frac{100}{60}$ s<sup>-1</sup>
- *T* = $\frac{60}{100}$= 0.6 s **[1 mark]**

Determine the angular velocity of the mass:

- *ω *= $\frac{2π}{T}$= $\frac{2π}{0.6}$ = 10.472 rad s<sup>–1 </sup>**[1 mark]**

Kinetic energy (and velocity) is maximum when displacement is zero:

- $E_{k}$=$\frac{1}{2}$*mv*<sup>2</sup>
- $v_{max}=ωx_{0}$* * where *x*<sub>0</sub>  is amplitude
- $E_{k}=\frac{1}{2}mω^{2}x_{0}^{2}$
- 0.5 = $\frac{1}{2}$× 0.42 × (10.472)<sup>2 </sup>× *x*<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup>

Rearrange for amplitude *x*<sub>0</sub> and substitute in the values:

- Amplitude, *x*<sub>0 </sub>=`square root of fraction numerator 2 cross times 0.5 over denominator 0.42 cross times open parentheses 10.472 close parentheses squared end fraction end root` = 0.147 m = 14.7 cm **[1 mark]**

Calculate the distance:

- Distance between the two maxima is twice the amplitude
- *d *= 14.7 × 2 = 29.3 = 29 cm (2 sf) **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *There are several useful formulae for the simple harmonic oscillation on the formula page. The equation *$v_{max}=ωx_{0}$* can be derived from:*

$v=\pmω\sqrt{x_{0}^{2}-x^{2}}$

> *by realising that speed is at a maximum at the equilibrium position, when **x**  is zero. Here, **x*<sub>*0*</sub>*  is maximum displacement (the amplitude).*

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

A mass of 0.42 kg is attached to a spring and the system is made to oscillate with simple harmonic motion (SHM) on a horizontal, frictionless surface. The mass passes through the equilibrium position 200 times per minute.

The experiment is moved to planet X. The gravitational acceleration on planet X is g$x$. It is known that  $\frac{g_{x}}{g}$ = 2. Another change is that three more identical springs are placed in parallel to the original spring.

The period of a spring undergoing simple harmonic oscillation is given by:

$T=2π\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}$

where *m*  is the mass of the object at the end of the spring and *k*  is the spring constant.

Describe, without calculations, how these changes affect the frequency with which the mass oscillates.
parts.solution_md:
Derive equation for frequency of a pendulum:

- *f =*$\frac{1}{T}$* *=  $\frac{1}{2π}\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}$

Consider the effect of a stronger gravitational field:

- Period is independent of gravitational acceleration / there is no *g* term, so change in *g* will not affect frequency; **[1 mark]**

Consider the effect of 3 additional springs in parallel:

- 4 springs will require 4 times the force to extend the same distance, so <u>*k*</u><u> in this experiment is quadrupled</u> (× 4); **[1 mark]**
- Frequency is proportional to $\sqrt{k}$, so the <u>frequency is doubled</u>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *The phrase 'without calculation' is your hint that the question wants you to use proportionality reasoning to answer this question. This is a really key skill in A level physics.*
